solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: How Donald talks about not roaming the hills (9)

indicators.note: Talking about something puts it in the middle of the talk, so QUACKS is wrapped round the other piece.
Letters that go roaming wander from their places, so NOT comes back in a new order.

explanation.surface: A duck grumbling about being kept off the hills.
explanation.walkthrough: The Quantocks are a range of hills in Somerset, England. 'Donald' is Donald Duck, whose talk is all quacking.
explanation.definitionFit: A proper name for a particular range: the Quantock Hills in Somerset are called the Quantocks for short.

clue.text: Land in Iraq, at Ar-Rutbah (5)

indicators.note: What is in the following words is contained by them, so the answer runs inside the letters of 'Iraq, at Ar-Rutbah'.

explanation.surface: Directions to a plot of land in a western Iraqi town.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is so Middle Eastern that a solver hunts for a region of Iraq; the neighbouring Gulf state is lying across the word breaks.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: Qatar is a country, and a country is a land.

clue.text: Like even an exam (2-5)

explanation.surface: Something described as being as flat as an exam.
explanation.walkthrough: An AS-level is an English school exam, the first half of a full A-level, taken at about 17.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the AS-level is one particular exam in the English school system.

clue.text: Listing of forbidden language about love (10)

indicators.note: About means around, so the language is placed around the love.

explanation.surface: A catalogue of banned words about love, as a censor might keep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forbidden language' reads as one idea, swear words; it is two pieces, and the forbidden piece takes the older spelling of taboo.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a tabulation sets items out in a table, which is a kind of listing.

clue.text: In burial site, weep and part (5)

blocks.note: PT is the standard abbreviation for part

explanation.surface: A mourner weeping at a graveside before going their separate way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part' is a verb in the surface, taking leave; here it is the noun, abbreviated.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a crypt is the vault beneath a church where the dead were laid.

clue.text: Helped to be made a fool of on the radio (9)

indicators.note: Radio is heard rather than read, so the answer only has to sound like the words it comes from.

blocks.note: to be suckered is to be made a fool of

explanation.surface: Someone helped into being mocked live on a radio show.
explanation.walkthrough: In a British accent, with the R silent, the two words are said the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense: to succour someone is to give them help in need.

clue.text: Tall building with many owners apart from English (5)

indicators.note: Everything apart from the E is kept, so that one letter is dropped from the word.

explanation.surface: A tower block in multiple ownership, none of the owners English.
explanation.walkthrough: The Shard is the tallest building in London, a glass spire by London Bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Shard is one particular skyscraper in London.

clue.text: Over-sleeps allotted time (4)

indicators.note: To turn something over is to flip it, so the word that follows is written backwards.

explanation.surface: Someone who oversleeps and eats into the time they were given.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over-sleeps' looks like one word; the hyphen splits off the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a span is a stretch of time, as in the life span one is allotted.

clue.text: Draw a sort of racing driver group together at the start (7)

indicators.note: Only what stands at the start of 'together' is used, its first letter.

blocks.note: the TT (Tourist Trophy) is the Isle of Man motorbike race
the RAC (Royal Automobile Club) is a British motorists' organisation

explanation.surface: An instruction to sketch a gathering of racing drivers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw' as a picture word keeps the solver thinking of sketches, not of pulling in.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to draw a crowd is to attract it, pulling it towards you.

clue.text: Irish town briefly supporting year-end event (9)

indicators.note: Said briefly, the town's name is cut short, losing its last letter.
In a down answer a supporter holds something up from below, so the town goes underneath.

blocks.note: ATHLONE, a town in the Irish midlands, without its E

explanation.surface: An Irish town sponsoring a New Year's Eve party.
explanation.walkthrough: The event is athletic, not a festivity: 'year-end event' is not one phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the decathlon is one particular athletics event, ten contests in two days.

clue.text: Where big lad can store his clothes? (7)

definitions.text: Where big lad can store his clothes?

blocks.note: read as asking about a large boy's room, and meant as the name of a thing: an adjective for big plus a word for lad
read as his wardrobe arrangements, and meant as a description of a piece of bedroom furniture with drawers

explanation.surface: Wondering where a large boy keeps his wardrobe.
explanation.walkthrough: A tallboy is a tall chest of drawers; read literally, it is a big lad, so it is where a 'tall boy' stores his clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: A tallboy is a high chest of drawers, furniture made for storing clothes, and its name also describes a big lad.

clue.text: Confused chapter about the ear holding answer (7)

indicators.note: Something holding another has it in its grasp, so the joined pieces keep the A inside them.

blocks.note: otic means relating to the ear

explanation.surface: A muddled section of a medical book about the ear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About the ear' is one piece, an adjective, not a container instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a chaotic scene is one in total confusion.

clue.text: Priest takes delight in this book of his (10)

explanation.surface: A clergyman's favourite book of the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This book of his' points to the Bible, a priest's book; Revelation is its last book.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Revelation is one book of the Bible, the book a priest works from.

clue.text: Limitless tax crushes son (4)

indicators.note: Something that crushes another closes in on it from all sides, so the tax surrounds the son.

explanation.surface: A son overwhelmed by an unlimited tax bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Limitless' reads as describing the tax; it is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: something vast is so large it seems to have no limits.

clue.text: Stupid jeer ruined witticism (3,7)

indicators.note: Something ruined is wrecked, and the letters are rebuilt from the wreckage in a new order.

explanation.surface: A dumb heckle spoiling someone's clever joke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stupid' looks like the anagram indicator; it is fodder, and 'ruined' does the work.
explanation.definitionFit: A borrowing from French: a jeu d'esprit, literally a game of the mind, is a light witty remark.

clue.text: Guide I needed through storyline (5)

indicators.note: What is needed through a thing runs through its middle, so I is threaded into the storyline.

explanation.surface: A writer admitting they need help finding their way through a plot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guide' could be a verb or noun in the surface; the answer works as either.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a pilot guides ships into harbour, and to pilot is to guide.

clue.text: Where one may find today’s crossword, or a collection of previous ones? (9)

definitions.text: Where one may find today’s crossword

blocks.clueFragment: Where one may find today’s crossword
blocks.note: two words run together: the newspaper, and the part of it where the Times puzzle is printed, its last page
a soft-covered book of old puzzles, as sold in bookshops

explanation.surface: A question about where to find the day's crossword.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense only works split in two: paper, then back.
explanation.definitionFit: The crossword runs on the back of the paper, and old puzzles are sold collected in paperback books.

clue.text: In great pain I left plant (9)

explanation.surface: Someone in agony abandoning a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' is the verb in the surface; here it is the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: tormentil is one particular plant, a small yellow-flowered herb of the rose family.

clue.text: Wrongly understood cut as another cut (9)

indicators.note: Something done wrongly is out of order, so the letters are rearranged.
A word that is cut is trimmed, here losing its final letter.

blocks.note: UNDERSTOOD, with the final D cut

explanation.surface: Someone misunderstanding a cut of meat as another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' appears twice: first as the trimming instruction, then in 'another cut', a cut of beef.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: tournedos is one particular cut of beef, a small round steak from the fillet.

clue.text: Put an end to villain’s parting urge (9)

indicators.note: To part something is to separate it, so the villain pushes into PROD and splits it.

explanation.surface: A scoundrel's last-minute urge before leaving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Villain's' is 'villain is': the rogue is doing the parting.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal term: a parliament that is prorogued has its session brought to an end without being dissolved.

clue.text: The side of the head (7)

blocks.note: read as part of the skull, and meant as a face of a coin
read as anatomy, and meant as the monarch's head, as in heads or tails

explanation.surface: A plain anatomical label: the side of someone's head.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'head' is on a coin, and heads is the obverse.
explanation.definitionFit: The obverse is the face of a coin bearing the principal design, usually a head, so it is the side of the head.

clue.text: Exhausted as horrid noise almost doubled (3,2)

definitions.note: exhausted as a verb, the past tense of did in

indicators.note: Almost the whole word means all but its last letter.
Something doubled is written twice, so the noise appears two times.

blocks.note: din = horrid noise, the second copy

explanation.surface: Worn out by a racket that was nearly twice as loud.
explanation.walkthrough: Did in is British informal for wore out.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: to do someone in is to wear them out, so did in means exhausted as a past-tense verb.

clue.text: Feature of kitchen artist captured in café (7)

indicators.note: Something captured in a place is held inside it, so the artist is shut up in the café.

explanation.surface: An artist caught on camera in a café's kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Captured' suggests a picture by the artist; it only means held inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a drainer, the rack beside the sink, is one fitting of a kitchen.

clue.text: For party it’s serious when leader is deposed (4)

indicators.note: A deposed leader is thrown out of first place, so the word loses its first letter.

explanation.surface: A political party in crisis once its leader is ousted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' and 'leader deposed' paint politics; the party here is for dancing.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a rave is one kind of party, a large all-night dance.

clue.text: Get to sit down too long? (10)

blocks.note: get as in 'I get it', to grasp a meaning
sitting too long means not standing enough: a prefix for too little, then the verb for getting on your feet

explanation.surface: Advice on catching sitting too long.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second sense as whimsical: under- as in underfed.
explanation.definitionFit: Get means understand in plain speech, and under-stand read literally means stand too little.

clue.text: Cross, once raves about potential reformer (2-3)

indicators.note: Someone who raves about is thrashing wildly, so the letters are thrown into a new order.

explanation.surface: An angry person ranting about someone who might reform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' tempts as EX; it is fodder, and the X comes from 'Cross'.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful description: a former prisoner is someone who may have reformed, or may yet.

clue.text: The retreat from Moscow? (5)

blocks.note: read as an army falling back, and meant as a quiet place to get away to
read as Napoleon's route home in 1812, and meant as where Muscovites go at weekends

explanation.surface: Napoleon's army falling back from Moscow in 1812.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase recalls Napoleon's retreat, a famous military disaster; the question mark admits the switch.
explanation.definitionFit: A dacha is a Russian country cottage, the place a city dweller retreats to from Moscow.

clue.text: Kitty adjudged to have nothing missing (4)

indicators.note: Having the nothing missing means the O is absent, so it comes out of the word.

explanation.surface: A cat judged to have nothing wrong with it.
explanation.walkthrough: Kitty looks like a cat; it is a pool of money.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a kitty is a pool of money collected for a shared purpose.

clue.text: Stuck in the past with a different circle (7)

indicators.note: With a different one in its place means a swap: one circle is exchanged for another.

blocks.note: ago = in the past; its O is the circle replaced

explanation.surface: Someone stuck in the past who moved to a new social set.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter O is itself a circle, which is what lets the setter swap it for another.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a ship that runs aground is stuck fast on the bottom.

clue.text: Very bad style worn by Ron (7)

indicators.note: Something worn by Ron goes round him like clothing, so the style wraps his name.

explanation.surface: A fashion verdict on Ron's terrible outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: Chronic for very bad is British slang, as in 'the service was chronic'.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional use: in informal British speech, chronic means very bad, beyond its medical sense of long-lasting.

clue.text: Manipulate requirement that’s voiced (5)

indicators.note: A word that is voiced is spoken aloud, so the answer only has to sound like it.

explanation.surface: A demand spoken aloud to control someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manipulate' suggests scheming; the sense is literal, working with the hands.
explanation.definitionFit: A literal sense: to knead dough or muscles is to manipulate them with the hands.

clue.text: Crazy rations with AA health farms (9)

indicators.note: Something crazy is out of its right order, so the letters are scrambled.

blocks.note: as written, joined to the fodder

explanation.surface: Wild diet rules at a health spa run like Alcoholics Anonymous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'AA' looks like the Automobile Association or Alcoholics Anonymous; it is just two letters of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: sanatoria, the plural of sanatorium, are places where people go to recover their health.
